text: Model chosen, dataset built and split — this is where it actually trains. This lesson wires LoRA and QLoRA, the forgetting-aware defaults from earlier in the course, and SFTTrainer into one runnable configuration on realistic single-GPU hardware. Nothing here is new in concept; the point of a capstone is seeing it all connect in one place instead of five separate lesson-sized examples.

Three earlier decisions plug directly into this run. Four-bit quantization makes an 8-billion-parameter model trainable on a single GPU. LoRA rank and target modules control how much capacity the adapter has. And a conservative epoch count applies the forgetting-aware ceiling from Chapter 4 directly, given a small, narrow dataset.

In code, that's a BitsAndBytesConfig for 4-bit NF4 quantization, a LoraConfig targeting the attention projections, and an SFTConfig with a typical LoRA learning rate and a capped epoch count — all passed into SFTTrainer along with the training split from last lesson. Calling train runs it, with logging and checkpointing happening automatically at the interval you configured.

Loss going down isn't sufficient on its own. Watch for the signature of overfitting on a small dataset — training loss still falling while held-out loss, computed periodically against the split you set aside, flattens or starts rising. Stop early if you see that, rather than training to a fixed epoch count regardless of what the curves say.

What gets saved is just the adapter — a few hundred megabytes, not a full copy of the base model, because the base weights stay frozen throughout, exactly as Lesson 27 described as PEFT's structural anti-forgetting advantage. Next up: evaluating this fine-tuned model against the pre-fine-tune baseline, using Chapter 7's methods.
